source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Imprecise Probabilities (Ellsberg case)
finding: Ellsberg urn: 30 red, 60 blue-or-yellow in unknown mix. Most people prefer red over blue and not-blue over not-red. No single probability fits both. An interval model fits: P(R)=1/3, P(B)=P(Y)=[0,2/3].
numbers: 90 marbles; 30 red; blue+yellow=60 unknown proportion.
limits: Steele notes the fit only works if the belief is truly indeterminate, not just badly introspected. Rival: Al-Najjar and Weinstein say people suspect the bet-offerer can rig the odds.
agent_relevance: Gives the cleanest case for a separate 'unknown' flag on a probability. A rival reading (suspicion of an adversary) matters for agents facing user-supplied bets.

source: SEP Imprecise Probabilities: weight of evidence (Keynes, Joyce)
finding: Fair coin vs coin of unknown bias both get P(H)=0.5 under a precise model. IP gives {0.5} versus [0,1]. This can explain preferring to bet on the fair coin.
numbers: Walley's proposal: interval width measures weight of evidence. It fails when evidence conflicts.
limits: Critics: resilience (Skyrms) or stability (Leitgeb) capture this inside precise probability. So intervals are not the only fix.
agent_relevance: A cheap alternative to intervals is a number plus a resilience tag: how much would new evidence move it.

source: SEP Imprecise Probabilities: suspension of judgement (Huber's measure)
finding: Huber measure I(X)=1-(lower P(X)+lower P(not X)) shows how silent the evidence is on X. Precise probabilism gives I(X)=0 always, so it can never express suspension.
numbers: Formula as stated in the entry. Elga's toothpaste case: max-entropy answers depend on how the options are described.
limits: Chandler: a precise probabilist cannot meet both uniform-treatment and re-description invariance (Y=1/X).
agent_relevance: An agent told 'use a uniform prior over the options' inherits this description-dependence. An 'unknown' flag avoids forcing a number.

source: SEP Imprecise Probabilities: dilation (White; Bradley; Steele; Hart and Titelbaum)
finding: Dilation: p(H)=p(Y)=1/2, H and X unrelated, yet P(H|Y)=[0,1]. Learning Y, which looks irrelevant, widens belief in H. Learning not-X does the same.
numbers: Interval goes from a point 1/2 to [0,1] after observing a cell of a partition.
limits: Bradley and Steele: the credal set changes, not just the interval for H, so no Reflection violation. Hart and Titelbaum: the problem is conditioning on a biconditional, awkward even for precise credence.
agent_relevance: Warns that 'widen the interval after new evidence' can be correct. A scaffold rule that says new evidence must narrow uncertainty is wrong in this class.

source: SEP Imprecise Probabilities: belief inertia
finding: If the prior for H1 is vacuous, every posterior is vacuous. The agent cannot learn from data.
numbers: Walley accepts vacuous posteriors as harmless. Rinard: vacuous priors are never legitimate states of belief.
limits: No numbers in the entry; fixes such as bounded priors are not quantified there.
agent_relevance: Hard limit on any 'unknown' flag: if unknown means total ignorance, evidence cannot update it. Use a bounded prior interval.

source: SEP Imprecise Probabilities: decision paralysis, regress, scoring rules
finding: Bets on a coin of unknown bias have expectation [0,1], so are incomparable. No real-valued scoring rule for imprecise probabilities is strictly proper (Seidenfeld, Schervish, Kadane).
numbers: Levinstein: the strict-propriety problem arises mainly for determinately imprecise, not indeterminate, credences.
limits: Williamson also asks why stop at sets: sets of sets or second-order probabilities. A second-order probability collapsed to its mean cannot fit Ellsberg choices.
agent_relevance: Brier-style scoring of an interval-reporting agent has no clean metric. Evaluate with width plus coverage, not one score.

source: SEP Imprecise Probabilities: empirical claims on ambiguity
finding: Ellsberg-type preferences are robust in many subjects (Camerer and Weber 1992; Fox and Tversky 1995). Some studies find them rarer than usually said (Binmore et al. 2012; Voorhoeve et al. 2016).
numbers: Entry gives no percentages. Neurological evidence discussed by Smithson and Pushkarskaya 2015, but stable neural structures for credence are controversial.
limits: Citations only; the primary papers were not opened by this agent.
agent_relevance: Human ambiguity aversion is real but not universal and depends on framing. Do not treat it as a target for the agent.

source: Elga (2010) Subjective probabilities should be sharp, Philosophers' Imprint 10(5)
finding: Sequential-bets argument. Bet A: lose $10 if H, win $15 otherwise. Bet B: win $15 if H, lose $10 otherwise. Accepting both guarantees +$5. Claims any rational agent accepts at least one, and that no permissive interval choice rule delivers this.
numbers: Worked case P(H)=[10%,80%]. Midpoint rule would value a $100 ticket on H at exactly $45 and so makes the interval pointless.
quote: Any perfectly rational agent who is sequentially offered bets A and B ... will accept at least one of the bets.
limits: Setup: full disclosure, no belief change, linear utility. SEP says Chandler and Sahlin-Weirich show a rule that forbids refusing both, and Elga noted this in an erratum. Bradley and Steele defend permissive rules.
agent_relevance: If the agent holds intervals it needs a decision rule that never rejects a free sure gain across a bet pair. Test this as a consistency check.

source: Kuzmics, Rogers, Zhang (2023) An Ellsberg paradox for ambiguity aversion, arXiv 2212.03603
finding: Lab design close to Ellsberg's two-colour urn: risky urn 49 white and 51 red, ambiguous urn 100 balls green or yellow. Subjects still choose the Ellsberg bet (white), but this choice breaks monotonicity, so classical ambiguity-aversion models cannot explain it.
numbers: 18 of 27 subjects (66.67%) made the Ellsberg choice; exact 95% Clopper-Pearson CI 46.04% to 83.48%. Same rate as traditional Ellsberg experiments.
limits: Small sample (27). Models that drop monotonicity (Seo 2009, Saito 2015, Bommier 2017, Ke and Zhang 2020) are not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Even the human effect the interval model was built for may not be about ambiguity. Weak ground for building agent behaviour on maxmin rules.

source: Oechssler and Roomets (2015) survey of 39 Ellsberg experiments, as quoted in Kuzmics et al. (2023) footnote 3
finding: Across 39 Ellsberg-type experiments plus their own, slightly more than half of subjects are classified as ambiguity averse.
numbers: 'Slightly more than half' of subjects on average. Exact count not given in the footnote I read.
limits: Second-hand quote; the original paper was not opened (fetch failed).
agent_relevance: About half of humans do not show ambiguity aversion, so human behaviour gives no single target.

source: Dembo, Kariv, Polisson, Quah (2026) Ever since Ellsberg, arXiv 2607.09355 (v2 Nov 2026)
finding: Revealed-preference test on portfolio choices (Ahn et al. 2014 data, 50 rounds, three states, one known probability). Choices are about as consistent with expected utility under uncertainty as under risk.
numbers: 154 subjects; 20 (13.0%) perfectly rationalizable by subjective EU. Fraction with consistency above 0.9 rises from 28.6% (subjective EU) to 50.0% (best of kinked or sophisticated) vs 68.2% for multiple priors. 42.9% better fit by kinked model, 44.8% by probabilistic sophistication.
limits: Heterogeneity is large across subjects. Data come from one older experiment.
agent_relevance: Roughly half of subjects fit a single-prior model as well as an ambiguity model. Intervals add fit mainly through free parameters.

source: Tak et al. (2026) Sparks of Rationality, arXiv 2601.22329 (ambiguity block)
finding: Ambiguity block: choose known 50/50 urn vs unknown urn with same payoff. Most reasoning LLMs show near-ceiling ambiguity aversion, far above typical human levels.
numbers: Measure AAI = P(choose known), 95% Clopper-Pearson intervals; stakes varied over a grid; Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Olmo3-7B and others, thinking on and off.
limits: Olmo3-7B instruct looked neutral only because it followed the random option order, not the task. Qwen3-8B was erratic across thinking on or off. Sadness steering lowered aversion only in Qwen3-4B and Olmo3-7B thinking.
agent_relevance: LLMs treat 'unspecified probability' as bad. Expect an agent to avoid unknown-odds options by default; an 'unknown' flag should be priced, not auto-penalised.

source: Tak et al. (2026) Sparks of Rationality: reasoning mode and expected-utility consistency
finding: Turning on thinking tokens makes models more consistent with expected utility, with weak loss aversion and near-linear probability weighting. Deviations remain: reversed endowment effect and near-complete ambiguity aversion.
numbers: No single headline figure in the part I read; see per-model figures in the paper.
limits: Small open models (4B to 8B class). In-context emotion priming stays near ceiling on ambiguity aversion; representation-level steering shifts choices toward neutrality.
agent_relevance: Reasoning helps on risk but not on ambiguity, so the ambiguity gap needs an explicit scaffold step if we want it.

source: Bini, Cong, Huang, Jin (2026) Behavioral Economics of AI: LLM Biases and Corrections, arXiv 2602.09362
finding: Question 6 is Ellsberg's two-urn test (Urn C known, Urn U unknown, $20 if black). Of four model families (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama), GPT and Llama answered 100% human-like (ambiguity averse), 0% rational.
numbers: Table row ambiguity aversion: GPT %rational 0.00 vs %human-like 1.00 (p<0.001); Llama 0.00 vs 1.00. Claude and Gemini cells did not parse cleanly in the text I extracted.
limits: Prompt asked for choice, confidence, a 50-word explanation, and intuitive-or-analytical tag. Number of repeated samples not read.
agent_relevance: Frontier LLMs are strongly ambiguity averse on the textbook stimulus. Treat as a known bias to correct or deliberately use.

source: Bini et al. (2026): pattern across model size
finding: Larger newer models are more rational on belief questions: Gemini 1.5 Pro answered all ten belief questions correctly; Gemini 1.5 Flash five; Gemini 1.0 Pro two. Preference questions show more human-like bias, including ambiguity aversion.
numbers: Ten belief-based questions per model; six preference questions; Claude 3 Haiku human-like on 3 of 6 preference questions.
limits: Preference results vary by question: GPT was rational on loss aversion but human-like on ambiguity.
agent_relevance: Scale fixes base-rate and sample-size errors but not ambiguity aversion. Handling of imprecise credence must come from the scaffold.

source: Hullermeier and Waegeman (2021) Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning, arXiv 1910.09457
finding: Argues standard probabilistic prediction conflates aleatoric (irreducible) and epistemic (reducible) uncertainty. Reviews methods that separate them, including set-based (credal) representations.
numbers: Abstract only read; no numbers.
limits: Survey, not an LLM study. Methods target classifiers and regressors.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for an 'unknown' flag: epistemic uncertainty is what more evidence can shrink.

source: Sale, Caprio, Hullermeier (2023) Is the volume of a credal set a good measure for epistemic uncertainty? arXiv 2306.09586
finding: Volume of a credal set is a sound epistemic uncertainty measure for binary classification. For more than two classes it loses properties: continuity fails and it is not robust, per the paper's Theorem 1.
numbers: Binary (d=2): volume behaves as expected and shrinks to 0 as data accumulates. d>2: continuity fails and small changes to the set change volume a lot.
limits: Theory plus toy examples; no LLM experiment.
agent_relevance: If an LLM agent reports intervals over many answer options, do not use interval volume as the unknown score; use per-option width instead.

source: Zucchet, Lee, Linderman (2026) Language models suffer from a curse of ambiguity, arXiv 2608.15448
finding: The more ambiguous a next-token distribution, the harder it is to learn: needs more capacity, larger embeddings, more fitting steps, and amplifies sampling noise. Shown on synthetic tasks with known ground truth and in models trained on real data.
numbers: No headline numbers read; claim is theoretical plus synthetic validation.
limits: 'Ambiguity' here means high-entropy outcome distributions, not Ellsberg-style missing probabilities. Easy to confuse.
agent_relevance: Model-stated probabilities are least accurate exactly where outcomes are most uncertain. Sample-based interval estimates will be noisy there.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know, arXiv 2207.05221
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false when format is right. Self-evaluation improves when the model sees many of its own samples. Models can be trained to predict P(I know), which transfers partly across tasks but is worse calibrated on new tasks.
numbers: Abstract only; no figures read. 36 authors.
limits: Calibration tied to format and to in-distribution tasks.
agent_relevance: A model-produced 'I do not know' flag is partially trustworthy, so it can supplement the interval idea cheaply.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? Confidence elicitation, arXiv 2306.13063
finding: Verbalized confidence from LLMs tends to be too high. Calibration and failure prediction improve with model capability. White-box methods beat black-box only slightly.
numbers: Five dataset types, five LLMs including GPT-4 and LLaMA 2 Chat; the abstract quotes AUROC 0.522 to 0.605, close to chance at the low end.
limits: Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Stated single-number confidence is weak. Hint that a range from several samples may beat a verbalized point value.

source: Keynes (1921) A Treatise on Probability
finding: Introduced weight of evidence as distinct from probability, and argued some probabilities are non-numerical or only comparable. Source of the two-urn contrast.
numbers: No experiment.
limits: Cited in SEP; not opened here. Content from memory.
agent_relevance: Origin of the idea that one number hides evidence amount.

source: Ellsberg (1961) Risk, ambiguity, and the Savage axioms, QJE 75
finding: Thought experiment with three-colour and two-colour urns. Preferences for known-odds bets over unknown-odds bets violate Savage's sure-thing principle.
numbers: Original was an informal survey of colleagues; not read here.
limits: Not opened. Modern lab: Kuzmics et al. 2023 found 66.67% of 27 subjects.
agent_relevance: The founding case for flagging 'unknown odds'.

source: Levi (1974, 1980, 1986) On indeterminate probabilities; The Enterprise of Knowledge; Hard Choices
finding: Credal state is a convex set of probabilities. Choice uses E-admissibility then a security rule; the agent may reject both Elga bets.
numbers: Bibliography entries confirmed in SEP; content from memory.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Source of the permissive choice rule Elga attacks.

source: Walley (1991) Statistical Reasoning with Imprecise Probabilities
finding: Lower and upper previsions; imprecise Dirichlet model; vacuous prior gives vacuous posterior (belief inertia).
numbers: No experiment.
limits: Not opened; claims partly confirmed in SEP.
agent_relevance: Possible template for a bounded-width unknown flag.

source: Seidenfeld and Wasserman (1993) Dilation for sets of probabilities, Annals of Statistics
finding: Showed dilation is common for imprecise sets: observing a partition can widen the interval for an event across broad model classes.
numbers: From memory; no figures.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Dilation is not a corner case.

source: Camerer and Weber (1992) Recent developments in modeling preferences: uncertainty and ambiguity, J Risk Uncertainty
finding: Classic review of ambiguity experiments; reported aversion mainly for moderate-to-high likelihood gains, weaker or reversed for low-likelihood gains (from memory).
numbers: Cited in SEP as showing robustness; numbers not read.
limits: Not opened; detail from memory, treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: If aversion depends on probability level, a flat penalty for unknown is wrong.
